opener.heading: Week 36: Community Helpers 🚚
about: Every day this week hands Azlyn a job that somebody in your town does for a living. She carries a mail route in a bag on her shoulder, draws the street from above and walks the map she drew, works a half-hour night shift by flashlight, and runs a lending library off the bottom shelf. Each job turns up with its own kit (a bag, a sign, a badge, a stamp), and the kit is what makes her believe in the work. Friday's bag comes back off the hook on Thursday, loaded with six cards for the six helpers she marked on Saturday's map.

Labor Day lands on Monday and gets a light touch. The morning washes the summer off the buckets and shuts them in a crate for the year, then Azlyn makes a picnic for the people who work in this house, serves it, and no adult gets up for an hour. Tuesday comes in hot, so that day bends around the heat: cold experiments in the morning, swimming at half past two, the middle of the day indoors.
azlyn: Carrying a load and adjusting it. Six parcels bend her sideways, and she takes one out at a time until she can walk the whole hall upright.
Matching a number to a place. Every parcel gets a number from 1 to 6, and one of the six houses down the hallway is the one that takes it.
Reading a map she drew herself. Six helpers placed in relation to home, then copied onto one sheet small enough to carry and walked with a crayon in her hand.
Sorting into categories she names. Every book in the house into four piles, labeled, shelved, and issued to you on a card she stamps.
Testing one thing at a time. Frozen washcloth, cold bowl, card fan, shade, cold drink, run one after another so she can tell you which one worked.
you: Carrying her own pack changes the walk
A map is a shift from being in a space to seeing it from above
Breaking the routine deliberately makes a memory
Endings need marking, and packing up does it
In serious heat, the physical problem comes before the behavior problem
Cozy is a real regulatory state rather than a mood
Being ill in summer is worse psychologically, and that's worth acknowledging
shopping: Cardboard boxes, 3 or 4 to flatten, plus one spare lid for the sign circle
Butcher or kraft paper, 6 feet, if you'd rather not cut boxes up
Shoeboxes or box lids, 7 (six houses on Friday, one card file on Wednesday)
Lidded crates or big boxes, 2 (the summer crate, the sick box)
A sturdy paper grocery bag with handles, or a cloth tote
A yellow or orange grocery bag, or an old adult t-shirt
An old belt, a bathrobe cord or 3 feet of thick string
Kitchen foil, or silver packing tape
Permanent markers, 3, at least one thick
1 pencil, if you are marking the door frame this month
Paintbrush, 1, and it goes in the paste
All-purpose flour, 3 tbsp for the paste
Blank cards or paper to fold into cards, 7
A wrapping paper tube, or a wooden spoon
A clipboard, or a hardback book to lean on
An alarm clock or a kitchen timer
Blankets or old towels for the windows, 2 or 3
A picnic blanket, and one small blanket per teddy
A clean glass jar, no lid
A nail brush or a sponge
Washcloths, 3 (two to freeze on Monday night, one clean for the sick box)
Small bowls, 2 (one for the paste, one for the sick box)
Juice, a pitcher's worth plus 1¼ cups for the popsicles
Popsicle molds, or paper cups and teaspoons
Fruit soft enough for her to cut (banana, strawberries, a pear)
Kitchen scales, if you have them
A cork, or a potato to halve for a stamp
A bell, or a spoon and a pan lid
A soft toy for the sick box
Six small things she can hold in one hand (soap, a spoon, a hairbrush, a ball of socks)
A small bag she can carry on Sunday's walk after dinner
opener.krestonNote: Kreston is 14 months this week. He scribbles with a whole fist, stacks two blocks and has three to five words he uses on purpose. He turns 15 months on Sunday the 5th, and from then he runs, spoons food into his own mouth and points at the pictures in a book.

days.title: The Bag on Her Shoulder
days.prepTonight: Put the grocery bag, the old belt, newspaper, packing tape and the marker on the kitchen table, and clear a space beside them for the six things she picks in the morning.

opening.title: What Goes Out Today
opening.need: newspaper · packing tape · 1 permanent marker · the 6 small things from the table.
steps: Six things on the table, each small enough for one hand: soap, a spoon, a hairbrush, a ball of socks. She picks them.
She wraps each one in a sheet of newspaper while you hold the tape. Lumpy is the correct shape for a parcel.
Number them 1 to 6 in marker, big enough to read from standing. All six have to be somewhere else by tonight.

main.title: The Bag That Holds the Whole Round
materials: 1 sturdy paper grocery bag with handles, or a cloth tote
1 old belt, a bathrobe cord or 3 feet of thick string
Kitchen scales, if you have them
steps: Tape the bag's base inside and out, and a strip round the top edge. Six parcels tear a paper bag out of its own bottom.
Thread the belt through both handles and buckle it, or knot the cord. Shorten it until the bag sits at her hip, then tape the crossing so it stops sliding.
She writes MAIL and her name on the side in marker.
Load all six and send her down the hall and back. Watch the shoulder drop and the lean come on.
Take one out and go again, until she walks the whole hall upright without stopping. Count what is left in.
Scrunch newspaper into the gap so the load stops swinging, weigh the bag on the scales, and write the number on the tape.
main.tip: She will stagger and refuse to take anything out. Let the walk fail twice before you suggest it. The number she reaches herself is the one she believes.

outside.title: The Card That Arrives After She Does
paras: Draw a card and address it to Azlyn at your own house, her name in full, then walk it to the blue collection box. September mornings still take bare arms and the hedges are full of blackberries, so allow a stop. Read her the collection times off the little door. The card lands on your own doorstep on Tuesday, because Monday is a day off for the people who carry it, and she has to wait for it.

days.infant: Kreston is 14 months and carries things while he walks, which is most of what he wants to do. Roll a dish towel, tape it into a parcel too big for his mouth, and hold your hand out for it. He brings it, you take it, he brings it again. Say mail each time it lands in your palm.

second.title: The Depot in the Hallway
second.intro: Six houses go down the hallway after lunch, and every parcel carries a number that has to match one of them.
materials: 3 feet of string to pull the basket
1 roll masking tape for the roads
A few of her toys as extra cargo
steps: Two strips of masking tape down the hall, a basket's width apart. That is the road, and the basket stays inside it.
Set the six boxes along one side, open ends to the road. She chalks a number on each, and you leave her backwards sixes alone.
Tie the string to the basket handle, knotted short so nothing trails. The basket is the truck and she drives it.
She reads the number on a parcel, drives to the house wearing it, posts it through. Wrong house happens. Let the householder complain.
Her toys go on as second-round cargo, each with a numbered strip of tape stuck to it in marker.
Run the round backwards: empty basket down the hall, collecting from every house with something to send.
Park the truck. She counts what came home.
second.tip: Give her one depot rule and hold to it. Nothing leaves without a number on it.

alternatives: Three houses and three parcels, on the kitchen floor.
Drop everything through the real mail slot from outside.
Sort the parcels by size, then by weight, and stop there.
Load the stroller and do the round around the yard.
outAgain: A friend's house, and the bag goes with her, loaded with something for whoever lives there
The café with the window seat, watching for anybody working outside
A walk past the collection box to see whether the pickup has been
Grandparents, and she delivers the parcels a second time
The road crew at the end of the street, and ten minutes watching over the fence

aroundWorld.title: Feeding the Workers Everywhere 🍱
paras: Getting a hot lunch to somebody at work is a job in itself. In Mumbai, dabbawalas collect stacked tin lunchboxes from home kitchens each morning and carry them across the city by bicycle and train. Sweden stops work twice a day for fika, coffee and a bun with everyone at the same table. A Japanese bento packs a whole meal into compartments small enough to carry onto a building site.
aroundWorld.tryIt: Stack her lunch instead of plating it. Two lidded tubs, one on the other, pasta below and something on top, tied in a dish towel and carried to whoever is working today.
aroundWorld.didYouKnow: Mumbai's dabbawalas move around 200,000 lunches a day and lose almost none of them.

days.krestonPM: He wants the basket. At 14 months in and out is the whole game, so give him a box of his own at the far end of the hall and two rolled dish towels to fill it with. He empties it and fills it again. The six numbered parcels stay on her round.

insight.headline: Carrying her own pack changes the walk.
paras: Azlyn will ask to be carried on an empty walk and cover half a mile with a loaded bag on her shoulder. A load hands her a job, and a job keeps a three-year-old moving, because the walk now has a point that belongs to her. Weight through her shoulders and back sends steady information about where her body is, and that settles her more than talk does. Keep the bag under a tenth of what she weighs, about three pounds, and let her load it herself. Parcels going to somebody else beat a bag of her own toys, every time.

days.safety: The bag strap. Keep it short enough that it cannot go over Kreston's head at 14 months, and take it off her before she climbs anything. The six numbered parcels are choke-size for him and they look like food, so they stay in her bag or in your hand and get counted back in before he is down on the floor. What he carries is a rolled dish towel, wider than his fist, and it comes back to your hand every time. Untie the string from the basket the moment the round finishes. September sun still burns on a walk with no shade: hat on, cream at eight, cream again at eleven.

days.title: The Street From Above
days.prepTonight: Trim two or three boxes square and leave them flat on the living room floor with the masking tape beside them, and cut one big circle from a spare box lid using a dinner plate as a guide.

opening.title: Looking Down From the Top Step
opening.need: the stairs · 2 toy cars · paper · crayons.
steps: Park the two cars at the bottom of the stairs and lie down beside them with her.
Go up and sit on the top step together. Same cars, and now she sees their roofs.
Hand her paper and a crayon up there and ask her to draw the cars from where she sits. Two rectangles is a right answer.

main.title: The Town Seen From Above
materials: The 2–3 trimmed cardboard sheets from last night, or 6 feet of butcher paper
1 sheet of paper for the walking copy
1 clipboard, or a hardback book to lean on
Sticky labels, or card scraps and tape
steps: Tape the sheets into one big sheet she can sit in the middle of. She holds each seam flat while you run the tape along it.
Ask where our house goes. She draws it there in marker, then tape the roads on: the road outside, a strip running to the store, junctions where she says there are junctions.
Mark the helpers: mailbox, store, fire station, doctor, the garbage truck stop by the house, the school crossing. A sticky label or a taped card scrap each, her drawing, your writing.
Crayon the garbage truck's route along the roads it takes past the house, with a cross at every stop.
Copy the six helpers onto the sheet of paper with the house in the middle. That is the walking copy, it goes on the clipboard, and the big one stays on the floor.
Hand her the cars. She drives the big map and tells you where she is going.
main.tip: The distances will be wrong and the store will end up beside the fire station. Leave it. She places things in relation to home.

outside.title: The Map on the Clipboard
paras: Take the walking copy out and walk the streets it covers, warm enough on the first Saturday in September to go slow. It sits on the clipboard and she holds it herself. At every place she marked, stand in front of the real one and let her put a crayon cross on the paper. Turn the clipboard with her at the corners.

days.infant: Kreston is 14 months and scribbles with a whole fist. Give him one crayon and the far corner of the map, and let whatever he puts there stay on it. He works flat on his belly longer than he works sitting up. Azlyn will name his marks as something within a day.

second.title: The Crossing She Runs Herself
second.intro: The crossing goes on the driveway after lunch and she works it. Everybody else does as they are told.
materials: 1 large cardboard circle, cut last night
1 wrapping paper tube, or a wooden spoon
Red, yellow and green paper, or paint
steps: Chalk the crossing across the top of the driveway, well in from the street: six fat bars, her width apart, with a waiting box at each end. She draws, you keep the line straight.
Tape red paper to one face of the circle, green to the other, then tape the circle to the tube, right round the join. Finger paint it instead if you would rather.
Tape a small yellow circle to the tube below the sign. Yellow means get ready, and she decides what counts as ready.
Push the toy cars along a chalked road towards the crossing and let her stop them with the red face.
Then real traffic: you with the stroller, Kreston on a hand, anybody else in the house. She holds it up and everybody obeys.
Swap. You take the sign, she takes the stroller, and now she watches for the color instead of showing it.
Sign indoors at the end, and the crossing goes onto the big map. She crayons six fat bars across the road beside the label she made this morning, so it is on the map as well as the driveway.
second.tip: Obey her the first ten times with no commentary. A sign held up by a small person still stops a grown-up.

alternatives: Chalk the crossing and skip the sign.
Drive the toy cars over the morning's map instead.
Chalk a parking lot and park everything with wheels in it.
Chalk round her shadow at the crossing, and again before dinner.
outAgain: The museum, first Saturday of the month, hunting anything seen from above: a model village, an aerial photograph, a floor plan
The upstairs window of the library, if yours has one over the street
A footbridge over a road or a railroad
The park, and up whatever she can climb to look down from
The top floor of a parking garage, and the streets laid out below
days.krestonPM: Twenty minutes on his own feet in the museum beats an hour in the carrier. At 14 months he stacks two blocks and he will find the one interactive drawer on the ground floor and open it forty times. Carry him past anything roped off.

insight.headline: A map is a shift from being in a space to seeing it from above.
paras: Azlyn has spent three years inside the street at knee height, learning it as a sequence of things she goes past. A map asks her to float above the lot and see it at once, and that change is one of the harder pieces of thinking available to her this year. She gets the landmarks long before the layout. The mailbox goes on the map because she remembers posting something, while the distances stay wrong for years yet. Hold the paper the way you are walking and turn it as you turn corners, and she keeps the two versions of the street attached.

days.safety: The crossing goes on the driveway, the path or the yard, never on a road, and say that out loud before the chalk comes out. A three-year-old carries the game to wherever she last played it. Work the top end of the driveway, keep yourself between both children and the street, and put Kreston on a hand or in the stroller with the brake on from the moment the door opens, because a car reversing out of a driveway sees neither of them. The sign sits at Kreston's face height, so keep a hand on the tube while she waves it. The walking map takes you out at eleven with no shade on the route: hat on, cream at eight, cream again at eleven. The scissors stay with you.

days.title: The Night Shift
days.prepTonight: Put fresh batteries in both flashlights and test them, fold two or three blankets by the window, and stand the basket of unmatched socks beside them.

opening.title: Who Is Awake While She Sleeps
steps: Tell her the true version of three in the morning here: everyone asleep, street empty, one car going past. Then ask who was awake somewhere else.
Write her list down the page word for word. Bakers, nurses, the man who drives the big truck, a cat.
She draws one of them at the bottom. The list stays on the table, because you need it at 9:15.

main.title: Working by Flashlight
materials: 2–3 blankets or towels for the windows
1 lidded cup of water for Kreston
1 alarm clock or a kitchen timer
steps: Blankets over the curtain rail or wedged into the frame, every light off, doors shut. Half past nine, and the room needs a flashlight.
Set the alarm clock for thirty minutes. That is the shift, and it ends when the bell goes.
One flashlight each. She can point hers anywhere she likes for the first two minutes.
Four jobs off her list by flashlight: match the sock basket, lay the silverware, find one red thing, carry Kreston's water through.
Sock matching is the hard one in the dark. Let two pairs go wrong and let her find out when the blankets come down.
At the bell, pull the blankets off together. Ask which job the dark made harder.
main.tip: Say the shift ends at the bell, then hold to it even if she is enjoying herself.

outside.title: Every Streetlight on the Way to the Corner
paras: Walk to the corner and back counting streetlights, stopping at each one long enough for her to touch the post. They are all off in warm September daylight. Ask who switches them on and let her theory stand. Count the row again on the way home, because you walk this stretch after dinner with a lantern.

days.infant: Kreston turns 15 months today. In the dark room this morning, put your flashlight spot on the wall and move it slow. He points at pictures in books at this age, and he will point at the spot and chase it. Say happy fifteen months out loud, because nobody else will.

second.title: The Jar Lantern for After Dinner
second.intro: The lantern has to be dry and lit by seven, so it gets built at one and left in a warm window while you are out.
materials: 1 battery tealight (a small flashlight does the same job)
1 small bag for the late walk
1 lidded cup and a drink for the walk
steps: Mix the flour and water in the small bowl until it looks like thin custard. She stirs, and it wants to be smooth.
She tears the tissue into palm-sized pieces. A torn edge lies flatter on the curve than a cut one.
Paste the jar with the brush, press the pieces on, then paste over the top. Two overlapping layers, and leave the rim bare.
Tie the string round the neck under the rim, both ends knotted into a short handle. Test the knot over the table.
Stand it on a warm windowsill and leave it there while you are out.
After dinner, drop the battery tealight in and turn the kitchen light off.
Pack the small bag for the walk: the second flashlight and something to drink. She carries the bag, an adult carries the lantern.
second.tip: Pajamas, shoes and out of the front door at seven is the part she tells people about. The whole thing takes fifteen minutes.

alternatives: Flashlight under a blanket with two books and nothing else.
A paper bag lantern with a flashlight inside, no paste.
Draw the night shift: a nurse, a baker and a driver.
Shadow puppets on the wall with the flashlight and her two hands.
outAgain: The sunset walk, scouted early, the route you take again at dusk, so she knows what is coming
The duck pond, counting how many are settling for the night
A slow walk with the stroller while Kreston runs the flat bits
The playground while the light is still high
The scooter along the flat stretch, so her legs are used before the late walk
days.krestonPM: He is 15 months today and he runs, so the late walk has him in the stroller or on a hand from the front door onward. Give him his own flashlight in the stroller and let him switch it on and off the whole way. He will sleep on the way home.

insight.headline: Breaking the routine deliberately makes a memory.
paras: Azlyn's days run on a shape she knows by heart, and a day that matches yesterday leaves nothing behind. Blankets over the windows at half past nine, dinner before a walk, out of the front door in pajamas: her brain marks the events that break the pattern and files them whole, while the ordinary ones blur into one average day. She will bring this Sunday up in November and remember none of last Tuesday. You need three or four of these a year, no more, and this one costs a flashlight, two blankets and one rule broken in front of her.

days.safety: No candle and no flame in the jar at any point, battery light or flashlight only. Azlyn wears something pale on the late walk and holds a hand at every curb, with you on the road side of her and Kreston in the stroller or on a hand from the front door onward. The jar stays up on the windowsill until after dinner and an adult carries it on the walk, and the string handle comes off it before it goes near Kreston. The streetlight walk runs in open September sun: hat on, cream at eight, cream again at eleven.

days.title: Packing Up the Summer
days.prepTonight: Stand the empty crate by the back door with the nail brush and the dish soap, and put two old towels where you can reach them without crossing the house wet.

schedule.label: Opening Activity
schedule.name: Everything That Lived Outside All Summer

schedule.label: Get Outside
schedule.name: Emptying the Pool Onto the Flower Bed

schedule.label: Wind-Down
schedule.name: Warm Bath After a Wet Day

opening.title: Everything That Lived Outside All Summer
opening.need: the yard · 1 empty crate or big box · her.
steps: Send her round the yard for everything that has been out there since June. Buckets, spades, water pistols, the chalk tub, one shoe.
Pile it on the patio in front of the crate. Say out loud that this is the last day it lives outside.
Ask which one she used most. That one goes on top, because it gets washed first at 9:15.

main.title: Washing the Summer Off Everything
materials: 1 lidded crate or a big box
steps: Two bowls on the patio, a stride apart. One warm and soapy, one plain for rinsing. She fills the second and carries it.
She washes with the nail brush and you take anything with mud welded on.
Rinse in the second bowl and stand each thing upside down on the first towel in the sun to drain.
Dry with the second towel and load the crate. She decides the order, and the biggest thing will go in last.
Write SUMMER and the year on the lid in marker. She adds her own mark beside it.
Tip both bowls over the grass the moment the last thing is dry, and let her carry them back in empty.
main.tip: Warm water, not hot, and give her twenty minutes of it before you press on with the crate.

outside.title: Emptying the Pool Onto the Flower Bed
paras: The kiddie pool goes today. Tip it a little at a time so she can see where the water runs, then aim the rest at the flower bed and the pot by the door, because it has been dry since August. She scrubs the inside with the same nail brush, and it gets folded onto the crate. Say goodbye to it out loud. She will want to.

days.infant: Kreston is 15 months and runs, and the words that hold him are the ones he is doing: wet, wash, gone. Give him his own small bowl with two inches of water and a spade in it, on the grass beside you. He tips it over himself within four minutes.

second.title: The Day Off Picnic
second.intro: Labor Day gives the people who work a day off. Azlyn makes lunch for the workers in this house, and then nobody does a job for an hour. If you are marking the frame this month, this is the afternoon for it. Pencil mark on the door frame, name and date, and her finger on the summer marks under it.
materials: Paper and crayons for the menu
1 pencil, if you are marking the door frame this month
steps: Tell her what today is in one sentence: everybody who works gets a day off, and that includes this house.
Menu first. She draws what is on offer and you write the words underneath in her order, spelling and all.
She butters the bread with the butter knife. Torn slices go on her own plate, which she will decide is fair.
Fillings on, tops on, and she cuts each round into halves. Aim for a wonky diagonal and praise it.
Fruit next: banana, strawberries, a soft pear, all of it cut by her with the same knife.
Load the tray. Plates, the pitcher of juice, a cup for everybody eating.
Blanket down on the grass or the living room floor. She serves, everybody sits, and no adult gets up for an hour. She will check.
second.tip: Take the hour as written. Lie down on the blanket and leave the phone in the house.

alternatives: Menu only, and a picnic of whatever is in the fridge.
Eat lunch on the floor with no plates at all.
Deliver a sandwich to a neighbor who is working today.
Blanket, cushions and a pile of books, and call that the day off.
outAgain: The green space with a ball, busier than usual with everybody off for Labor Day
The riverside path, counting the people out who would be at work
The playground, late enough that the heat has come off it
A slow walk with the stroller and nothing to achieve
The yard with the sprinkler on for the last time this year
days.krestonPM: At 15 months he spoons food into his own mouth and gets about half of it there. A picnic blanket is the best floor for that. Give him his own plate and a spoon and let the rate of loss go unremarked.

insight.headline: Endings need marking, and packing up does it.
paras: Summer ends for Azlyn the moment somebody tells her it has, and a sentence is thin evidence. Washing the buckets, drying them and shutting the lid hands her the ending in a form she can hold: the things went away, she put them there, the season is behind the lid. Three-year-olds run on episodes rather than calendars, and a small ceremony at the close of one lets her file it. She may want the crate open again on Thursday. Open it. The marking has done its work either way, and next March she will remember the day it came back out.

days.safety: Standing water. Kreston is 15 months and runs, and a dishpan on the ground holds enough to drown in. Tip the bowls and the pool out the moment you are done with them, and stay within arm's reach of him the whole time water is out. A wet patio is slick under her feet, so the carrying happens at a walk. The morning runs outdoors start to finish, so hat on, cream at eight, cream again at eleven.

days.title: Working in the Heat
days.prepTonight: Soak two washcloths, wring them out, fold them flat and put them in the freezer, and fill an ice cube tray. Swim bag by the door.

schedule.name: Which One Cools Her Down Fastest

schedule.label: Get Outside
schedule.name: Hand on the Path, Hand on the Grass

schedule.label: Second Main Event
schedule.name: The Jacket You Can See From a Long Way Off

opening.title: The Washcloths in the Freezer
steps: Open the freezer and let her take both washcloths out. Stiff as boards, and she has not met that before.
One on a plate on the table to thaw where she can watch it, one back in for 9:15.
Ask her to name every way she knows of getting cooler. Take the list as it comes, then open the windows on the shady side.

main.title: Which One Cools Her Down Fastest
materials: 1 washcloth, still frozen from last night
2 pieces of thick card for fans
Paper and a marker for the chart
steps: Chart first. Five rows down the paper, and she draws at the head of each: washcloth, bowl, fan, fence, cup.
The frozen washcloth on the back of her neck for a count of twenty, then one foot, then the other. One washcloth, three places, and she says which one she felt first.
Bowl of cold water on the patio with a handful of ice cubes in. Both feet in, twenty seconds, out.
A piece of card each. She fans your face and you fan hers.
Out to the shade by the fence with nothing in her hands. Chalk round the edge of the shade while she stands in it.
Back into the sun for the last one, a cold cup out of the pitcher, drunk where the sun is. Then to the chart, and she marks her winner in marker, any shape she likes.
main.tip: Run these one at a time with a gap between. Do them together and she cannot tell which one worked.

outside.title: Hand on the Path, Hand on the Grass
paras: Out before eleven and back before the heat sets in. Flat palm on the paving slab in the sun, then on the grass a step away, then the metal gate and the wooden fence. Same sunshine, four answers, and she will not believe the gate until she touches it. Walk the shadiest route home and let her pick the shade at every corner.

days.infant: Kreston is 15 months and runs, which makes him hotter than her and less able to say so. Hat on, water offered every fifteen minutes whether or not he asks, and no bare feet on the paving. Hand him the thawing washcloth off the plate for two seconds, cool rather than stinging, and watch his face do the whole report.

second.title: The Jacket You Can See From a Long Way Off
second.intro: Every helper she has watched this week wears one. Hers comes out of a carrier bag, and the whole job happens at the table and on the hall floor, because the hall is the coolest strip of the house at one o'clock.
materials: 1 yellow or orange grocery bag, or an old adult t-shirt
Kitchen foil, or silver packing tape
1 piece of card for the sign
steps: Lay the bag flat on the table, cut the base seam open, then cut a slit down the middle of one face so it does up like a jacket.
Cut an armhole out of each side, high up. Hold it against her shoulders first and cut small.
She tries it on, and masking tape takes in the shoulders wherever it gapes. It comes straight back off, because sealed plastic holds heat.
Tear the foil into four strips as long as her arm. Two across the chest, two across the back, taped at both ends.
She draws on the card, you write STOP in letters she can copy, and it stays in her hand.
Six paper cups upside down along the hallway are the cones. She draws a stripe round each one in marker and sets them out in a line.

Jacket on, and she closes a lane on the hall floor. Everybody who comes past gets stopped, held and waved on, and the stroller goes through the gap she leaves. The cones go out onto the path at quarter past four, when the heat has come off it.
second.tip: A grocery bag holds heat like a greenhouse, so the jacket goes on for the lane and comes off between jobs. Foil beats a drawn silver stripe because it flashes when she moves, and dusk is when she gets to see that.

alternatives: Cones only, six cups down the hall and the ride-on round them.
Tape foil strips to a t-shirt she owns and skip the cutting.
Badge and sign only, and she works the kitchen doorway.
Write STOP in outline and let her fill the letters in with crayon.
outAgain: Swimming, and the best place to be at half past two in September heat
The shallow end and nothing else, if the pool is packed
A splash pad or the kiddie pool at home, if the pool is shut
The shady half of the park, and home before four
A cold drink somewhere with air conditioning, if she is done in by three
days.krestonPM: Twenty minutes in the water is plenty at 15 months, and he will be cold before he looks it. He runs on the poolside now, so keep a hand on him out there. Hold him facing you for the first minute in, then let him kick.

insight.headline: In serious heat, the physical problem comes before the behavior problem.
paras: A hot afternoon produces a version of Azlyn nobody can reason with, and the heat arrives before the tantrum does. Small bodies carry more skin for their size, start sweating later than yours, and warm up three to five times faster. Watch for the flushed, floppy, gone-quiet child rather than the loud one, because quiet is the one that matters. Fluid goes in before she asks for it, since thirst turns up once she is already short. Meet the body first with a cold drink, a wet washcloth and shade, then find out what the argument was about. Half of it will have gone.

days.safety: A patio dishpan holds enough to drown a running 15-month-old, so Kreston stays inside arm's reach every minute it holds water and it gets tipped out the moment the cooling job is done. September heat. Cream on both of them before the door opens, and again before the pool: hat on, cream at eight, cream again at eleven. Paving, metal slides and buckle clasps burn small hands at these temperatures, so test each one with the back of your hand first, and if you cannot hold it there it comes off bare feet and bare hands. Fluid into both of them early, and keep the middle of the day indoors. The jacket is sealed plastic and holds heat against her, so it comes off between jobs and never goes on outdoors before four. The scissors stay with you. Swimming this afternoon. Both children stay within arm's reach in the water at all times, and no float or seat is a substitute for your hands.

days.title: The Librarian
days.prepTonight: Halve a potato and leave it cut side down on a plate, stand the shoebox and the index cards on the table, and clear the bottom shelf of whatever is on it now.

schedule.label: Opening Activity
schedule.name: Bringing All the Books to One Place

schedule.label: The Main Event
schedule.name: The Lending Library on the Bottom Shelf

schedule.label: Wind-Down
schedule.name: Three Books From Her Own Library

opening.title: Bringing All the Books to One Place
opening.need: every book in the house · 1 laundry basket or a big bag.
steps: Give her the basket and a route: her room, the car, under the sofa, the pile by your bed, the one in the bathroom.
She tips the lot out in the middle of the floor. A three-year-old sitting in a heap of every book she owns is worth the mess.
Ask how many she thinks there are, count the first ten together, and leave the rest for quarter past nine.

main.title: The Lending Library on the Bottom Shelf
materials: Every book in the house, in a heap
About 20 index cards, or card cut to size
1 cork or the half potato as a stamp, and a little paint on a saucer
steps: Four piles, and she decides what they are. Scary ones, animal ones, Kreston's, long ones.
Four index cards for the labels. She draws, you write her words underneath in marker, and they tape along the shelf edge.
Ten books get a pocket: an index card taped inside the back cover along three edges, top left open.
She stamps each pocket with the cork or the potato, dipped in the paint on the saucer. One stamp each is the rule.
One borrower card per person in the house, name in marker, hers drawn on in crayon. They live in the shoebox.
Shelve all four piles on the bottom shelf, labels out, low enough for her and Kreston to help themselves.
main.tip: Let her issue you a book before anything gets tidied away. Card out of the pocket, into the shoebox, and she names the day you bring it back.

outside.title: Two Books Under a Tree
paras: Two books go out in the bag and get read under a tree. Pick the shade, because early September still runs warm by eleven and the leaves are turning at the edges without being down yet. Sit on the grass with your back against the trunk. She reads one to you first, whatever version comes out, then you read the other. Both come home, because they are library property now.

days.infant: Kreston is 15 months and points at pictures, which is the whole of reading at his age. Let him have the second book on the grass and follow his finger. Name what he lands on, wait, and name it again if he points twice. Azlyn will take the naming over, and she is better at his pace than you are.

second.title: Story Hour on the Rug
second.intro: The library opens at one o'clock and she runs the story hour. The audience is Kreston, the teddies and whoever else is in the house.
materials: 1 rug and every cushion in the room
1 bell, or a spoon and a pan lid
Card and tape for a badge and a sign
steps: Badge first, because she is not a librarian without one. Card, her name in her own marks, taped to her sweater.
A sign for the door: STORY HOUR, drawn by her and taped up at her height.
She sets the room. Every cushion out of the sofa, a chair per teddy, a blanket each, and the rug for the audience.
She picks three books off her own shelf and stands them face out where the audience can see them.
Bell to start. One ring, everybody sits, and nobody talks over the librarian.
She tells the pictures. She cannot read the words and does not need to, and her version runs longer than the printed one.
Bell to finish, then a second sitting for anybody who missed the first. She will want three.
second.tip: Sit on the floor and be an audience member. Put your hand up to ask a question and she will run the room for an hour.

alternatives: One blanket, one cushion, one book, on the sofa.
Read to Kreston through the stairgate and let him choose by pointing.
Sort every book by size, tallest to smallest along the shelf.
Build a den out of the cushions and read inside it.
outAgain: The indoor play center, cooler than the park by mid afternoon, and she needs the noise after a quiet hour
The library itself, if you would rather see the real thing this week
Indoor playground, if the play center is full of the after-school crowd
The park in the shade with two of her own books in the bag
A thrift store, and she chooses one book for the shelf
days.krestonPM: He is 15 months and runs, so the play center is the right shape of afternoon for him. Stay with him in the under-twos area and let him do one thing forty times over. Back home he goes to the bottom shelf on his own.

insight.headline: Cozy is a real regulatory state rather than a mood.
paras: Cushions, a blanket each and a rug make Azlyn easier to be around, and there is a mechanism under that. Warmth and light pressure on the skin push her toward the settled end of her nervous system, and a small bounded space cuts down how much she has to filter at once. She will sit through a story on the rug that she would leave halfway through at the table. Her body settles first and language gets her attention after that, in that order. Build the nest, then open the book, and story hour runs twice as long as you planned for.

days.safety: The cork and the potato half are choke-size for Kreston at 15 months, so they go back on the counter between stamps and never onto the floor. Washable paint only, because the shelf he now helps himself from is the one she has been stamping over. Halve the potato yourself with the knife, and the cut half goes in the trash at the end of the day rather than back in the fruit bowl. An hour under a tree still burns fair skin in early September: hat on, cream at eight, cream again at eleven.

days.title: The People Who Make You Better
days.prepTonight: Take every tablet, bottle and packet out of the first aid box and lock them away or put them high, then stand the box on the table with a tray beside it. Set the lidded box, the clean washcloth, the plastic bowl, the popsicle molds, the soft toy and the fresh box of bandages out beside the tray.

schedule.label: Opening Activity
schedule.name: What's in the First Aid Box

schedule.label: Get Outside
schedule.name: Spotting the Signs That Mean Help

schedule.label: Second Main Event
schedule.name: The Last Delivery of the Week

schedule.label: Wind-Down
schedule.name: Bath, and the Week's Map Taken Down

opening.title: What's in the First Aid Box
opening.need: the emptied first aid box · 1 tray · 1 trash bag.
steps: Tip what is left onto the tray. Bandages, bandages, a triangle of cloth nobody has ever used, tweezers you keep hold of.
She sorts it in two: things that go on the outside of a person and things that do not. You read the dates, and the old ones go in the trash bag.
Everything usable goes back in. Tell her the next box she packs is for the inside of a person.

main.title: The Sick Box
materials: 3 books kept out of yesterday's shelf
Popsicle molds, or paper cups and teaspoons
steps: Give her the job in one line: the next person here to be ill gets this box, and she packs it while everybody is well.
Popsicles first, since they need the time. She fills the molds with juice, or paper cups with a teaspoon standing in each, then into the freezer.
Washcloth folded into the bowl, bowl into the box. Tell her what the bowl is for.
Three books off her shelf, held back yesterday. She picks the ones she would want read to her.
Soft toy in, sealed box of bandages in, both in a corner where nothing squashes them.
Card last. She draws for whoever opens the box, you write her message word for word, and THE SICK BOX goes on the lid in marker.
main.tip: Do not let her have the popsicles today. The box works because it stays shut.

outside.title: Spotting the Signs That Mean Help
paras: Walk with one job: find the signs that mean somebody can help you. The pharmacy sign, the AED cabinet inside the grocery store entrance, the sign over the doctor's office, the fire hydrant at the curb with its cap painted. Stand at each one and say what it means in a sentence. She finds the hydrants first.

days.infant: Kreston is 15 months and points at everything at chest height and below, which is where these signs sit. Follow his finger and name what he lands on, even when it is a drain. He runs now, so the pharmacy doorway and the curb both want a hand on him.

second.title: The Last Delivery of the Week
second.intro: Six cards go out this afternoon, one for each helper she marked on Saturday's map, and Friday's bag comes off the hook to carry them.
materials: Card or paper, folded into 6 cards
steps: Map on the floor. She finds the six places she labeled on Saturday: mailbox, store, fire station, doctor, the garbage truck stop, the crossing.
Fold six sheets in half, one card each, and she chooses which helper gets which.
She draws. One picture per card, made for the person who does that job.
Ask what she wants to say to each one and write it inside in marker, word for word. Do not tidy her grammar.
Cards into envelopes, and she licks and presses every one shut. The ones going in the mailbox get a stamp top right, and she puts them on.
Mend the bag strap with masking tape where it has torn, load the cards in and hang it on her shoulder.
Deliver on the way to the post office. Mail the stamped ones, hand the others over in person, and let her do the handing over.
second.tip: Call the doctor's office or the fire station first and ask whether a three-year-old can drop something in. Most places say yes.

alternatives: Two cards instead of six, and post both.
Draw one big picture for the garbage crew and tape it in the front window.
Make a get well card for the sick box instead.
Deliver to the neighbors on foot and skip the stamps.
outAgain: The post office, with the six cards and the errand you have been putting off all week
The corner store, and she hands a card to whoever is behind the register
A walk past the fire station to see whether the doors are open
The bakery, and she chooses something for tomorrow morning
The pharmacy counter, and she hands a card to whoever is filling the orders
days.krestonPM: A post office line at 15 months is a long five minutes. Give him one envelope to carry and hand over. Let him run the last stretch home.

insight.headline: Being ill in summer is worse psychologically, and that's worth acknowledging.
paras: Being ill in February costs Azlyn nothing she wanted. Being ill in the first warm week of September costs her the garden, the pool and whoever is outside without her. Three-year-olds have no way to weigh one lost day against all the ones still coming, so a sunny sick day reads to her as everything, gone. Saying it out loud, that this is a rotten deal and she is missing the good weather, does more for her than distraction, because it puts you on her side of the complaint. The box she packed today hands the ill version of her something chosen by the well one.

days.safety: Take every medicine out of the first aid box before she sorts it and put it back somewhere locked or high, not into the box she now plays with. Check the dates yourself. Bandages, packets and small tubes are choke-size for Kreston at 15 months and he will follow her straight to the box, so the sorting happens on the table with him in the high chair, and the box goes up on a high shelf between sessions. The hydrant and the pharmacy door both sit at the curb: hold his hand from the curb onward, keep yourself between both children and the traffic, and read the signs from the sidewalk rather than the edge. Hat on, cream at eight, cream again at eleven.
